Walter de Maria: On the Importance
of Natural Disasters. (May 1960)

I think natural disasters have been looked upon in
the wrong way.

Newspapers always say they are bad. a shame.

I like natural disasters and I think that they may be the highest
form of art possible to experience.

For one thing they are impersonal.

I don't think art can stand up to nature.

Put the best object you know next to the grand canyon, niagra falls,
the red woods.

The big things always win.

Now just think of a flood, forest fire, tornado, earthquake, Typhoon,
sand storm.

Think of the breaking of the Ice jams. Crunch.

If all of the people who go to museums could just feel an earthquake.

Not to mention the sky and the ocean.

But it is in the unpredictable disasters that the highest forms are
realized.

They are rare and we should be thankful for them.
[In: Young (ed.): An Anthology, 1963.]

Ben Vautier: Accidents and Catastrophes. (June
1961)

The plastic beauty of certain photos of catastrophes,
of accidents, led me in June 1961 to set my signature to the crushed
and tangled bodywork of a car that had hit a tree.



Then, carried away by my creative élan, I signed:

AGADIR: Earthquake (board carrying documentation).




FRÉJUS: The dam which, giving way, caused the death of 300
people.



HIROSHIMA: As I remember is one of the most successful examples
of this category of artwork created by the genius of man, and even
if artistic intention was lacking, we can only congratulate ourselves
on its esthetic reality.
[In: Vautier, 1963]
